discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: Dry conditions expected today with an upper level ridge positioned over the region. Areas of fog will be the main concern today and again Saturday morning before the next system arrives by Saturday evening. This system will bring light lowland rain and mountain snow to western Washington. The pattern will become more active next week as a series of systems brings widespread precipitation, gusty winds, and the potential for minor coastal flooding.

sections.title: Update
paragraphs: No changes made in this morning's update. The previous discussion remains below:

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Dry conditions expected today with an upper level ridge positioned over the region. Areas of fog will be the main concern today and again Saturday morning before the next system arrives by Saturday evening. This system will bring light lowland rain and mountain snow to western Washington. The pattern will become more active next week as a series of systems brings widespread precipitation, gusty winds, and the potential for minor coastal flooding.

sections.title: Short term (today through Sunday)
paragraphs: A ridge will build into the region today as an upper level low over Oregon and northern California moves off to the south and east. Conditions are cool out there this morning with temperatures trending in the low to mid 30s as of 1AM/09Z. A few spots, especially areas south of the Sound, may see morning lows dip down into the upper 20s. Areas of fog have also started to develop across the Chehalis Valley this morning with light winds and ample moisture in the low levels. Freezing fog is likely for colder spots across the Southwest Interior overnight, with fog expected to expand further northward across Puget Sound through the early morning hours. Dry conditions are expected with the ridge overhead, with fog expected to lift and scatter by the afternoon. Afternoon highs will be in the mid to upper 40s across the interior and into the low 50s along the coast today.

Another round of fog (and freezing fog) is expected by Saturday morning, with lows expected to dip back into the upper 20s to mid 30s across the area. The ridge will then push further inland in the morning, allowing for an upper level low to drop southward from the NE Pacific and position itself offshore through Sunday. This system will bring the next round of light rain to the lowlands and light snow to the mountains. Rain will approach the coast by late Saturday morning and then gradually push inland into the interior by late afternoon. Overall rainfall amounts will remain rather light through Sunday, with only a few hundredths of an inch expected for the interior lowlands and around a tenth of an inch expected along the Central Coast. With snow levels hovering around 2000 ft, could even see some light snow accumulations (less than 1 inch) at the Cascade passes. Afternoon high temperatures both days will be in the mid 40s to low 50s. Lastly, high astronomical tides over the weekend may bring the potential for some minor coastal flooding along the Pacific Coast and the Strait of Juan de Fuca by Sunday.

sections.title: Long term (Sunday night through Thursday)
paragraphs: The low situated offshore will eventually become absorbed into the mean flow on Monday as a broad upper level low drops down into the NE Pacific from the Aleutians. This low will then deepen offshore Monday night into Tuesday and will bring a more active pattern to western Washington as the system swings a number of disturbances across the region. Expect multiple rounds of widespread lowland rain, mountain snow, and gusty winds through the second half of the week. Additionally, high astronomical tides combined with the weather impacts from these systems, will increase the threat for coastal flooding - most notably along the Pacific Coast as large waves build along the coast Tuesday into Wednesday.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Gradual improvement to VFR is beginning for terminals impacted by fog. A slow lift to IFR is being met for widespread VFR picks up after 21z. Mid to high clouds should help limit fog formation Saturday morning to the southern interior (OLM). Light to calm winds this morning, will increase this afternoon to 5-6 kt.

KSEA...LIFR cigs this morning. VFR this afternoon once the fog scatters out. Mid to high clouds will move in this afternoon but fog is remaining favorable to form again tonight into Saturday morning. Light southeasterly winds this morning at 5 kt or less, increasing to 5-7 kt this afternoon.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Generally benign marine conditions today with weak high pressure over the waters. Fog may form over the interior waters, with highest chances over Puget Sound this morning. Latest high-res guidance suggests portions of the Central and South Sound has a 50-60% chance for seeing visibilities less than 1 NM.

A low pressure system offshore will bring elevated seas and winds to the waters starting as early as tonight through this weekend. A Small Craft Advisory has been issued for the coastal waters and West Portion of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Additionally, as the front associated with the parent low passes over the coastal waters, winds will increase toward gale force over the outer waters Saturday morning. With latest high-res probabilities around 50-70%, a Gale Watch has been issued for the outer coastal waters. As for the inner coastal waters, confidence is much lower for gale force gusts, but may see an occasional gale gust. Seas will build towards 10-13 feet by Sunday.

An active weather pattern will continue next week. A stronger system will impact the waters Monday into Tuesday. Increased offshore winds are highly likely to bring additional headlines. Confidence continues to increase for the potential for gales and storm force winds over the coastal waters. Latest model guidance now highlights probabilities higher than 70% for gales starting late Monday morning. Winds look to peak early Tuesday morning, with high confidence (90% and higher) for gales and a 45-70% chance for storm force winds over the outer coastal waters. Additionally, there is a 50-70% chance for gales through the Strait of Juan de Fuca on Tuesday and a slight chance (35-40%) for an isolated storm force gust through the Central and East Strait. Seas will build towards 20 feet over the outer coastal waters, with probabilities suggesting a 25-35% chance for seas exceeding 20 feet.

Additional headlines are favored midweek into late in the week, with a 70-100% chance of small craft winds over the coastal waters and Strait of Juan de Fuca. Seas are likely to remain elevated as well, with probabilities above 70% for seas greater than 10 feet and a 40- 70% for seas greater than 15 feet.

sections.title: Hydrology
paragraphs: Wetter systems moving into the region next week will start to bring some rises to area rivers. At this time, no widespread river flooding is expected, however the Skokomish River will likely cross into flood stage mid to late week.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: Dry weather continues into Saturday morning before an active weather pattern returns. A series of Pacific frontal systems will bring multiple rounds of rain, mountain snow, and breezy winds starting midday Saturday and continuing through next week.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Dry weather continues into Saturday morning before an active weather pattern returns. A series of Pacific frontal systems will bring multiple rounds of rain, mountain snow, and breezy winds starting midday Saturday and continuing through next week.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Thursday...Visible satellite imagery early Friday afternoon depicts widespread stratus that had formed overnight slowly dissipating from southeast to northwest across NW OR and SW WA as weak, transient high pressure forms over the region. Stratus may not dissipate completely from far NW OR and SW WA before the sun sets, so these locations may end up with high temperatures a few degrees lower than forecast. Otherwise, high temperatures this afternoon one again are forecast to peak in the mid 40s across the Willamette Valley, 50s along the coast, and 30s along the Cascades. As the high pressure moves inland overnight, there's the potential for another round of fog/stratus forming tomorrow morning, though high clouds moving in ahead of the next weather system could limit that formation.

Today is the last dry day in the forecast through at least Thanksgiving Day. Multiple weather systems are slated to move through the PacNW through next week, bringing the return of a wet pattern. Precipitation returns Saturday as an upper level trough deepens in the eastern Pacific and pushes a frontal system inland tomorrow night into Sunday. Rain is forecast to begin along the coast by late Saturday morning, pushing inland as scattered showers over the afternoon, continuing into Sunday. Latest guidance indicates that the low will spin offshore through the day Sunday before moving northeast and weakening offshore of WA/BC on Monday. Because of this pattern of the low staying offshore, precipitation chances and amounts have decreased inland from yesterday's guidance, with higher precipitation chances of 70-95% over the Coast Range, Willapa Hills, and Coast. This has impacted the Cascade snow forecast, as well. Although snow levels will be around 2500-3500 ft, QPF amounts over these elevations will mainly be less than 0.1-0.25 inch. Therefore, the probability of snow amounts of at least 2 inches is now only 20-40% at pass level for Saturday through Sunday and less than 5% for 4 inches. For elevations higher than pass level, there's a 40-70% chance of at least 2 inches and 15-40% chance for at least 4 inches. Those who have outdoor plans over the high Cascades should still plan on snow covered roads at times, especially in stronger showers.

Ensemble guidance is in good agreement that another low pressure system will deepen in the eastern Pacific early next week, hot on the heels of the weekend system. Ensembles suggest this system will also spin offshore through much of the week, likely pushing multiple frontal systems inland through the week. The next frontal system bringing widespread rain and a period of breezy winds to the region will be late Monday into Wednesday. This system will have more Pacific moisture associated with it than the weekend system with latest ensembles indicating IVT values peaking around 500-750 kg/(ms). From late Monday through 4 AM PT on Thursday, there's a 60-80% chance of at least 1 inch of rain along the coast, 40-70% over the Cascades, and 25-60% for the inland valley, with highest probabilities around and north of the Columbia River. Looking at probabilities for at least 2 inches, those drop to 35-50% along the coast, 10-45% over the Cascades, and 5-20% for the inland valley. No significant flooding impacts are expected at this time, though periods of heavier rain could cause localized ponding of water in lower lying areas. Breezy winds are possible along the coast with the frontal passage on Tuesday, as well. There's a 40-65% chance of peak wind gusts at least 45 mph and a 5-20% chance for peak gusts at least 55 mph.

Beyond Wednesday, ensemble guidance becomes more uncertain on specific details of the low pressure system, though precipitation chances continue through at least Thanksgiving day. There is the indication that another frontal system may push into the region sometime Thursday into late week, causing another round of widespread rain and breezy winds. NBM has a 15-30% chance of peak wind gusts of 55 mph or higher on both Thursday and Friday with a 30-60% chance of at least 1 inch of rain across all of NW OR and SW WA for the 48 hour period ending at 4 AM PT Saturday. Keep an eye on the forecast, especially if you have travel plans for the upcoming holiday. -03

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 00Z Saturday...Satellite imagery and terminal observations as of early Friday afternoon depicts MVFR stratus across the central and northern Willamette Valley while conditions have cleared out along the coast and southern Valley (KEUG). Given the low sun angle at this time of year, there is low confidence for stratus clearing out across Portland/Vancouver Metro area terminals. Will likely maintain MVFR CIGs across these areas through the rest of the afternoon. Based on satellite, KSLE may clear out in the next hour to VFR. Terminals that clear out will maintain VFR conditions through the rest of the evening.

Tonight, expect another round of low stratus across the Valley, however, there is uncertainty with how low stratus will get. High pressure briefly moves overhead tonight, and if it produces a strong inversion, it can result in IFR/MVFR stratus. Guidance suggests a 30-50% chance for IFR CIGs across parts of the Valley at any given hour between 09-16z Sat. Variable winds around 5 kt or less continue through this evening. East/southeasterly winds increase after 12-15z Sat along the coast and KTTD as pressure gradients tighten ahead of the next system.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...High-end MVFR (2-3 kft) and low-end VFR CIGs prevail through this evening. 20-40% chance for IFR CIGs at any given hour between 10-15z Sat. Southwesterly winds around 5 kt or less through 00-01z Sat, then turning easterly through the rest of the TAF period.    -10

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Light southerly winds around 15 kt or less continue across the waters through this evening with seas around 5-6 ft at 11 seconds. The next frontal system arrives late tonight into Saturday, increasing southerly winds with gusts up to 30 kt. Small Craft Advisories are in effect tonight through early Sunday morning. For the outer waters beyond 10-20 NM offshore, isolated gale force wind gusts up to 35 kt are possible. Guidance did not suggest that gales would be frequent or widespread enough to warrant a Gale Warning. High confidence (70-90% chance) for seas building to 8-10 ft on Saturday, and 12-14 ft by Sunday.

Active weather continues next week as a series of systems impacts the waters. There is potential for storm force wind gusts early next week, with a 60-80% chance for at least isolated wind gusts exceeding 48 kt across the outer waters beyond 10 NM offshore. In addition, seas will also build into the mid to upper teens, with a 20-40% chance of exceeding 20 ft on Tuesday for areas beyond 30 NM offshore. For the Columbia River Bar, chances for seas exceeding 20 ft are currently around 5-15%.
Long period swells will also result in a moderate threat for sneaker waves through this weekend. Those visiting the coast should use extra precaution when in or near the water.     -10
